text: The House will come to order. Members, please take your seats. Sergeant-at-Arms. The House is now in session. All personnel not entitled to the privileges of the four, please retire to the gallery.

The members will arise and be led in prayer by Dr. Steve J. Collins, Appalachian School of Theology, Nicholsville, and remain standing for the Pledge of Allegiance to the Flag of the United States of America, which will be led by the Delegate from Alexandria, Delegate Herring. Good afternoon. Shall we pray?
Gracious and Sovereign Lord, we just want to thank you for this opportunity to gather with these, our fellow Virginians. And what a heritage that we share and what a legacy that we have to fulfill.

So we come to you today, lifting our members of the House of Delegates up to you because you are the giver of all wisdom. And we ask that you would grant them clear minds and discerning hearts as they make decisions that affect many lives.

give them strength to serve with integrity courage to do what is right even when it is difficult and humility to seek the common good of all men rather than their personal gain lord guide them with your truth steady them with your peace amid pressure division and uncertainty surround them with wise counsel protect them and their families and remind them that true authority is found in

serving others well may their work promote justice peace and human flourishing around the commonwealth and even throughout our entire nation so we entrust them to you asking that your will be done in our commonwealth for your glory and for the good of all people in jesus name we pray amen amen

Delegate from Scott County, Delegate Kilgore. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Rise for an introduction. Delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I hope you'll join with me in welcoming Dr. Steve Collins, who delivered our invocation this morning. Dr. Collins serves as a pastor of the First Baptist Church in Nicholsville, Virginia, has a great ministry all over Southwest Virginia.

He's the president of the Appalachian School of Theology in Nicholsville, which opened a second location in Uganda this past September. The school in Uganda has over 8,000 students. So we really appreciate the mission work that Dr. Collins and his school are doing in Uganda.
So he and his wife, Sandy, live in Dungannon in Scott County, Virginia. I hope that you will join me in welcoming Dr. Collins to the house. Welcome, Dr. Collins.

Welcome to the Capitol today. The delegate from Richmond City, Delegate Cousins. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise for an introduction. The delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. in the gallery today, we have the second grade class from Anna Julia Cooper School along with their teacher and chaperones. I ask that they please stand. Anna Julia Cooper School is a tuition-free independent school for K-8 students in Richmond's East End, dedicated to uplifting its students and graduates through an education founded on love. The school is named after Anna Julia Cooper, who was born into slavery in 1858,

who was an educator, an author, an activist, and one of the most prominent African-American scholars in US history, and who viewed learning as a means of true liberation. In honoring its namesake, AJC provides students with exceptional education, wraparound services, extracurriculars, athletics, summer camps, and graduation support to students into high school and through adulthood.
I request that members join me in extending a warm House welcome. Welcome. Welcome to the Capitol today.

Delegate from Newport News, Delegate Price. Mr. Speaker, I rise for the purpose of an introduction. Delegate, ask the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, with us today, as is his usual custom. We have the congressional representative for the 3rd Congressional District, who is the ranking member of the Education and Workforce Committee and um a former member of this august body and then got a little crazy and decided to join that other body down the hall but he's a fierce advocate and so i would love for us to give a warm house
welcome to congressman bobby scott of the third congressional district welcome welcome welcome congressman scott and uh you got the natives riled up this morning pursuant to house rule 30 the

journal shall reflect that the following members are away on pressing personal business and are granted leave from today's session, Delegates Garrett, Knight, Lauffer, and Runyon. Clerk will announce the next autobiography. Mr. Speaker, in the second portion of the morning hour is not applicable given today's calendar. Same for the third portion of the calendar as well.

Clerk shall announce the next autobiography. And the fourth and final portion of the morning hour is reserved for member requests for points of personal privilege. The delegate from Fairfax, Delegate Boulevard. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Rise for a point of personal privilege. The delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker and members of the body. I'm cognizant that this is a Friday and everybody is excited about the inaugural activities. This is also, I think, my third point of personal privilege in the 20 years that I've been here. My first one was when my

grandfather passed away. He was a Marine who fought in Okinawa and Iwo Jima as a World War II veteran. The second one was a very, very passionate, impromptu speech I gave on recycling rates. in the Commonwealth of Virginia.

I know that that's a pretty famous one, and I'm sure people still talk about it today. I've also been around long enough to see a lot of different farewell speeches. And so I've seen really funny ones. I've seen very, very serious ones.

I've seen ones where there's a lot of unsolicited advice given to each and every one of you. But I also know that the best ones are the shortest ones. And so I'll try to keep this as brief as I can. And that is, after all, it isn't the farewell speech that I will remember or you will remember.

The exception might be Riley Ingram's very, very infamous farewell speech, which was a tell-all. If you are new to the chamber, you should really go back and take a look. There were a lot of nervous people here on the House floor. But it's the interactions, it's the adventures, it's the laughs, it's the late nights, And honestly, it's the occasional tears that I think we've had together that we will all ultimately remember.

Mr. Speaker, I remember walking through these doors for the very first time and thinking about the weight of history. And I know you've mentioned that many times, and I think each of us have felt that very same weight. And I also think about the awesome responsibility we have, not just to current Virginians, but for generations after generations to come.

I look at my children today, the oldest of which were only six and eight when I was first elected. One of them didn't exist when I was first elected. And at the forefront of my mind as I've taken literally thousands of votes sitting in this chamber is what kind of world would I leave for them?

But those are my children. I think the truly sobering thought is that I and all of us shape the lives of other people's children. Millions of parents and children we will never meet. and that is truly an awesome responsibility.

I am keenly aware and very humbled that my journey and any successes that I might have had along the way are because of the dedication and efforts of many, many people. To those who have worked so hard on my behalf for the last 20 years, thank you.

You've made it possible for me to represent the community that I grew up in and the community that I deeply love, and words cannot express my gratitude and my appreciation. Special thanks to my long-term legislative assistant, Rama Van Pelt, who has been here with me for those 20 years.

He is an incredible partner, the quintessential professional, and he has worked behind the scenes on literally thousands of constituent issues and requests. And so if he's watching right now, thank you, Rama. I want to thank and recognize the incredible House staff.

Mr. Clerk, you and your team are amazing. To all the fantastic and dedicated people of the Division of Legislative Services who work over the holidays and late into the evening to get those bills right, thank you. Our committee staff are as wonders at keeping things moving along.

I want to especially thank my General Law's Clerk, George Cain, and our Senior Staff Attorney, Ashley Binns. You made us look really good despite ourselves. And on appropriations, a debt of gratitude to all of our staff.

But I especially want to thank Ann Oman, Kim McKay, and David Reynolds. I have learned so much from each and every one of you. And then to my amazing wife, Gretchen, my best friend and partner in life. Ever since we first met at Robinson Secondary, I knew that we would have amazing adventures together.

And when I would have doubts, you were always there to support me, gently pushing me when I needed extra encouragement. You have been a true partner every step of the way, and I'm looking forward to being there for you in your next role. To my children, Alex, Josette, and Grayson, I am very proud of you.

I know that growing up in a political family is not easy, but I hope you know that it meant the world to me that we did this together. And thank you as well to those who might not have always agreed with me, but nonetheless offered friendship and a different perspective.

That honest discussion and collegiality have been deeply valued. And one of the most meaningful things that was ever said to be by a member of this body is that while I may not always agree with you, I trust you. And finally, my deep gratitude to the residents of the 11th House District, who have entrusted me to be their voice for the past two decades.

Mr. Speaker, at a recent event, you mentioned my involvement in the emergency committee, for which I deeply appreciate that you allowed me to be chair of that committee and to take the show on the road all across Virginia. And then you said, part of the reason for selecting me is because I was as boring as watching C-SPAN.
Sorry. To which my wife turned to me and said, what's wrong with C-SPAN? We love that channel. Mr. Speaker, thank you for placing your trust with me.
In closing, I love this house, and it has been an honor to serve with each and every one of you. Thank you.
Delegate from Chesapeake, Delegate Lefwich.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise for a point of personal privilege. Delegate, ask the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I'd like to address the retirement of Delegate Bulova. I've known this delegate for a long time. I've worked with him while we had a supermajority. I worked with him while we had a slim majority, I think through a coin toss.

I've worked with him when the other side of the aisle had a slim majority, and I was actually looking forward to working with him while y'all had a supermajority. I've known him as a member of his committee on general laws, and then he got to be on the committee when I was the chairman of general laws.

And both of those transitions were very smooth, and I attribute that to his integrity and honesty and trustworthiness. I was struck by something he said when he was getting ready to retire, when he gave his retirement speech. And he talked about the impression or the effect you have on other people's children.

And I would say to him that he did that best through the way he conducted his life and the way he handled himself as a person and an individual. And lastly, what I'll say is, you know, we're all part of our own little clique and group.

And when I go home, being a Republican, I hang around Republicans for the most part, the city committee meetings and stuff. And many people come up to me and say, oh, my gosh, you know, what those people are doing in Richmond. I say, wait a minute, hold on, stop. They're good people.

There are a lot of people on the other side of the aisle that I have a tremendous respect for, even though we may disagree on things. I say they're good people. they believe they just have a different way of approaching that and whenever i said that there was a picture in my in my dictionary of of a few people that uh really thought the most of that that about and the delegate that was retiring is one of those people uh tremendous tremendous respect for this man and i'm very sorry to see him go although i wish him well in his new endeavors
the delegate from arlington delegate lopez thank you speaker point of rise for a point of personal privilege? Delegate has the floor. What can you say about a guy you've known since high school?

We all know him, in the elegant words of Delegate Leftwich, as someone who is respected and generous and in the weeds on public policy and the sort of epitome of what a delegate should be. I knew him originally in high school as an incredibly cool rockabilly punk rocker. And if you ask him today, who his best favorite bands are, it'll surprise you. That being said, there's a reason

why several of us joke, even when there was a super majority on the other side, you could bet your next mortgage payment that David Bolovo was going to pass three water bills in the first 10 days of session, at least three. And it's because of who he is. Because as we all believe, you can trust him. He gets into the weeds on data. He gets in the weeds on policy. He's talking to all

parties. And he has a great opportunity, both professionally and personally, and in his public service journey right now. But to say that you will be missed and that you are deeply appreciated is an understatement, a massive understatement. And I hope we all can sort of strive to be the

kind of legislator that David has always been, which is kind and generous and caring and really in the weeds on public policy and who's coming at everything from a people perspective, not about whether or not it's a Republican idea or a Democratic idea, but whether or not it's a good idea that'll help families in Virginia. And I'm going to cry again, and I'm not going to do that, but thank you

for your example. Thank you for your friendship. And thank you for all the work you've done in the General Assembly. And may we all strive to be trusted the way David Boulava is trusted. The delegate from Richmond City, Delegate Jones. Mr. Speaker, I rise for a point of personal

privilege. The delegate has the floor. I haven't been here as long as Delegate Boulava and those that are leaving this August body today. But a good friend of mine said you don't have to be eternal to be effective, and that's the one thing I've sought to do. Without a long speech, the one thing I know how to do is preach from an ancient text, and Mr. Speaker, there's one text that comes to mind, to whom much is given, much is required, but the way it ends, it says, and even more will be

asked, and Mr. Speaker, that's something you've lived by, that's something that you've done in our time together and my time here in this body. You've always asked more of not only yourself, but all of us, not just Democrats, not just Republicans, but this entire body. I've had the privilege to watch history unfold. And I meant that when I talked about my mother's scrapbook a couple of years ago, that it's a privilege and it's been an honor to be a part of Virginia history, which is a part of your life story. And that is something that has been a guiding light
in the North Star, as I've dealt with the last session, facing prostate cancer and dealing with that. This is more than just a body of legislators. We've built friendships.

I was still in Johns Hopkins University Hospital, and two people called me, our speaker and our chair. I was high as a kite. I can tell. But I know that they called, and that is something I will never forget.

forget and so I appreciate you and all that you do when when when he came to my first launch party he didn't talk about the job that he wanted me to do he just gave a phone number 280-332-281-330-8004 hit Mike Jones up on the low because Mike Jones is about to blow and I knew something was different about this man right there anyone with his position and his aspirations to come in and be that real and that transparent meant something to me because that's something I've tried to

endeavor to do as a pastor and a politician. To all the leaders, Leader Tran or Leader Herring and Chair Tran, thank you for y'all's compassion and the boot, the gentle boot that would make sure that we were supposed to be where we needed to be as long as we needed to be there.

To all of those that embraced our class, we looked up to so many of you as we read the newspaper of what's going on in the General Assembly, as we saw what was going on in the Richmond area and the Commonwealth. We looked up to so many of you, and many of you were so much larger than life.

And it was just, it's been a privilege to just sit next to you and to listen and to hear all of the wisdom that came from your lips, your mouths, to share with how you do policy the right way. To my class, I think I have one of the best classes the General Assembly's ever seen.

We came in, D's and R's. We had a great relationship, my friend Chad Green. Personal trials, tribulations, he was one of the first ones to call. And even in his absence, I can still recognize and share that he is a friend, someone who I care deeply about and wish him the best.
Whether it was the powerful speeches that our class did or using sign language to share a deep message, we are a talented and gifted class. And I'm just so glad to be a small part of that.

You know, going through the whole special election, the whole process, you know, people were concerned with, would you lose? There was no losing. I would either go to the Senate because the vote said so or i would come back to a 64 seat majority that's a win-win and i'm gonna miss that i'm surrounded by chesterfield chesterfield and henrico we didn't have that when i first came in and that's something that we've all fought to do and we've done it together and so i want to challenge you to continue to lead with love compassion and conviction and do the work that

we've been called to do by those that have voted us into this place. To the constituents of HD 77, I leave you in good hands of Delegate Elect Charlie Schmidt. I've known him for a while, and I'm looking forward to the work that he does, because if he doesn't do it, I'll see him on crossover. And so I wish him the best. I wish him the best in what he has to do. There's an old hymn that we would sing in the church mama mcquinn we are soldiers in the army we have to fight although
we have to die we have to hold up that bloodstained banner and we'll still hold it up for the day we die i'll see y'all all at crossover god bless you i'm not clapping for you as long you ain't going

nowhere um the delegate from colonial heights delegate jerry mr speaker i rise for a point of personal privilege the delegate has the floor thank you mr speaker um we have a lot of names we use for each other in this body.

Some of them good, some of them not. All of us are colleagues with one another because our constituents have sent us into this place to represent them. Many of you over time, we develop into friends because we share those committees, we share those ideals, we talk about the things that we find value in.
We talk about our shared struggles, our cares. And periodically it goes a little bit deeper than that. And I'll use the term brother for my friend.

Mike Jones. We bonded over a shared love of sport, whether it was high school football, various basketball teams. We shared life together when we had struggles with our families and with other things that were going on around us. So very rarely is it that we get to get that depth of familiarity with someone in such a short time as we spent in this chamber together.

But I always knew where he stood. I always knew where he was because we had an open channel of communication, and we would work across that center aisle, no matter the majority, no matter the minority, no matter what the situation or circumstance was. Now, as you said, we're not getting rid of him, Mr. Speaker. You know, many times when we give these farewell speeches, we don't know if we'll ever see that individual again. They may live in a far southwest or north part of the state, and I try not to go north of Fredericksburg if I can help it. But we know

we're going to see him again, whether that be at the other end of the hallway or at the other end of the bench that he's now on the losing team in the basketball game. So the fact that he's choosing to go to that other august body down the hall, sometimes, Mr. Speaker, when people want to be wrong, you let them be wrong, and you get out of their way. But I say thank you for being my

colleague, for being my friend, and for being my brother. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The delegate from Virginia Beach, delegate, ask you. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, I rise to the point of personal privilege. The delegate has the floor. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Speaker, you know this versus him pretty well.

I'm quite sure that the delegate from Richmond knows it too. So I'm going to start my speech with a question to the outgoing delegate. And I'm sure he's heard a lot of times in 20 years. I'm going to do a little help, a little crowd participation. So, who? Mike Jones. Who? Mike Jones. There we go, there we go.

Or better known as, in the future, as Senator Mike Jones. Mike, while you will no longer be in this chamber, you won't be too far away. As you just stated, we'll see you at Crossover. While in this body, you fought to protect our communities by banning auto seers. You fought to protect our athletes at practice by making sure they were hydrated and protecting them from exhaustion.

You worked to protect our communities, Richmond, from a lot of traffic fatalities, as we've seen over the past few weeks and lost community members. But Mike, you've always been a listener ear. You will no longer be around the corner for me to bother you and steal your sodas, but I promise you I'll be down to talk about life and for you to mentor me as an older brother, and I greatly appreciate those conversations.

You know, we thank you for your continued service to this Commonwealth from your time on the City Council to your time here in the House of Delegates. And we will miss you here in this body. So thank you again. Thank you for your service to work with you. A lot of members here will be bothering you as it comes close to crossover.

And we appreciate your kindness as we head into that. And you said is I don't I hope you don't mind if I give out your number for the for the Commonwealth again. But if you ever need to reach him, again, that's 281-330-8004.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Delegate from Fairfax, Delegate Sickles.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I rise for a point of personal privilege. Delegate has the floor. Thank you. My first advice to everybody is don't leave on the same day as these other great people leave on. It is not good. I wanted to say something about David, Delegate Boulevard, because I sat beside him several times.

And for the new people, he read every bill. He knew every bill. So I cheated a lot. He told me what it was about. I had a million questions for him. He never got tired of answering them. So anyway, good luck saving the environment and doing all those good things you're going to do for us.
He's wanted to do this his whole career, and now he's going to get a chance to make a big difference. To Delegate Jones, we've sent a lot of delegates down the hall. It hasn't helped yet.

So maybe you're the one. Maybe you're the one. I hope so. So as as Delegate Bulba said, I've listened to many of these speeches over the years. You will not remember this and it will be mercifully short. I've been here a long time. I was appointed to Delegate Lacey Putney's P&E committee in 2004.

He was such a gentleman. At the first committee meeting, he told us why P&E was not only the first committee, but also the most important committee in the General Assembly. Everything else flows from our elections. Delegate Putney stayed for 22 years like me. Then he stayed another 30 years after that.

One farewell speech I remember was your predecessor a few times removed, Mr. Speaker. I had not been here that long when Kenny Melvin announced he was not running again. I was bummed because I saw the difference he could make in our deep minority.
He left after 24 years here. And I have to have a lot of people to thank, many on the other side. Speaker Howe put me on appropriations when we only had seven members on our side.
So I know how that feels. I feel for you. I don't feel that bad. I spent 18 of 22 years in the minority. It's a lot less work if you want it to be.

And in other ways, it's harder because you need to work harder to get things done. So good luck over there. As a reminder to those who ask how we did it all those years, we did some very important things in a minority.

For example, our votes were critical, telling you to talk to our side over here, to the passage of Speaker House transformative transportation legislation 2013. That could not have been done without Democrats on our side.

the bill would not have emerged from the Finance Committee without Democrats. The Speaker, this is a secret, don't tell anybody, but the Speaker lobbied our members to get the votes to get it out of Finance Committee. And if you want to know what a difference that bill has made, there's a guy named Nick Donahue getting on board soon, and he will tell you, because he is an encyclopedic, has an encyclopedic knowledge of everything.

It has been transformative for our state, for the economics of our state, and we're still benefiting from it every day. And, of course, Medicaid expansion in 2018, when we had 49 on this side, what a difference expansion has made for not only the working poor in Virginia, but for every person in the Commonwealth, because in health care, everything is related to everything else.

And that's what we learned, and that's what we're, unfortunately, having trouble with now, understanding as our historically low uninsured rate is threatened. Didn't mean to put that policy stuff in there, but I thought I'd take a shot anyway. These were great achievements, but I wouldn't trade these victories for the progress we made in our majority for anything.

I'm looking forward, Mr. Speaker, to watching all you can do over the next at least four years with this historic administration that will be sworn in tomorrow. I'd also like to thank, as my colleague Boulevard did, Chairman Torian and the outstanding staff on the 12th floor for the education of a lifetime.

For those of you new to appropriations, it is a different committee. If you are unhappy, if you don't get your way or your perfect bill, you should immediately ask the Speaker to put you on another committee. You can go to county, cities, and towns or something.
Well, sorry. Well, I mean, I know that's a tough committee, but it's not quite the same. When I started, former Chair Chris Jones welcomed any legislator who would do the work.

The budget is largely bipartisan. Nobody in either party wants to waste precious General Fund dollars, so it is always an annual opportunity to work together. So, Mr. Speaker, I will miss serving you in this body, serving with you in this body, or serving you, too.

And thank you for all your kindnesses. And I've said before, if you can get the ice cream machine working downstairs, you will see me more often. So, thank you. And a shout-out to my current chief of staff, Andrew Millen, in the gallery for all the work you did.
All my former aides seem to be doing a lot better than I ever did, and I'm proud of all of them. So thank you, Mr. Speaker, and good luck.
Speaker.

The delegate from Falk Hill County, Delegate Weber. Mr. Speaker, I rise for a point of personal privilege. The delegate at the floor. I've got to gather what I was going to say because Delegate Sickles did such a great job.

Mr. Speaker, over the course of the time that I've been here, I've gotten to know quite a lot of people. A lot of people, you don't realize, the longer you are here for the newbies, you will see how many people come and go.

Before and after, and when you start looking at your license plate number, you're like, all right, did he come in after me? Did he come in before and after? You know, you're like, all right, well, after today, I move up two more slots. Just saying. There's still somebody else, I believe, that's also going to step away today, too.

So I'll try and do all of them that I can real quick, because I will tell you some lessons that I learned from each of them. And when I first got to this body, someone told me to get to know all 100 of your colleagues because each of them will teach you something.

And I've tried to take that to heart. And there's 100 of us, so it gets a little difficult, I guess. You have to do it over time. But my classmate, Alfonso Lopez, about David Bolivar was absolutely correct.

I still remember coming in. I think I carried five bills my first year. That's why I was. And I got one through. One. Small government Republican. Just saying. But I watched David stand up, I'm sorry, Delegate Bolova stand up, Mr. Speaker, and it would be a slew of bills right before crossover.

And I'm like, how did he get all this stuff done? And it's because he always chose projects that just, they were needed, they were bipartisan, and they were for his district. And he would just, it was local issue after local issue after local issue.

And I think what I learned from that was when you pick issues, we're going to have issues that we're going to battle over. But always find an issue where you can reach across the aisle and get to know your colleague because at some point there's going to be issues that we're going to come together on, period.

For Delegate Sickles, I will tell you that if I ever wanted to get into the minutiae on the budget, particularly with health care, I would, when you were sitting where Vivian is sitting, I would stop and spend about a half an hour.

But I will tell you that when it came to any program and you wanted an honest opinion about what it was going to do or what money was needed or any of that, it was always Delegate Sickles that I could trust to get back to Delegate Bolivar's issue.

Now, I'm going to talk about Mr. Jones. I don't know why you want to go down the hall. And Delegate Sickles is absolutely right. We have sent a number of delegates down there, and it still doesn't help us. But congratulations. You have conducted your business with fortitude and reason, and I look forward to seeing that further.
And if I could, Mr. Speaker, I would like to address a delegate that I battled with on a number of different occasions.
Not as much as Nick Freitas battled her. But it was always in committee, either Commerce and Labor or Labor and Commerce, depending on which side you're talking.

Or Melissa Police and Public Safety when she first got here. but I will tell you that the partisan rancor that you see today and that we experience in this body at times, I, this summer, reflected on her loss. And I will tell you that despite the fact that we, as I posted, fought like cats and dogs, it was always those moments at 11 o'clock at night
working on energy bills or doing something else where you found the humanity that we miss when you literally watch television and I will honestly say that I learned a lot from you.

I learned a lot from every single one of the members that are leaving this body and I learned a lot about tenacity and strength and I will say that each one of us in this body whether you're here as long as Doug at Sickles in Bolivar which is a long time or you decide you want to go across the aisle or down the hall the history of this body the average person will never

see. But the impact that we have will last forever. And it was Delegate Torian that this summer basically said even if you're here for a short time, you can leave an impact. And I have a feeling we're going to be seeing the impact from this summer, this session. So Mr. Speaker, I just have to say thank you to my colleagues. Thank you for your service. And thank you for the education that
you gave me. Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Delegate from Fairfax, Delegate Tran. Thank you so much, Mr. Speaker. I rise for a point of personal privilege. The delegate has the floor. Thank you.

When I first came into this house, Delegate Sickles was assigned to be my mentor. How lucky was I? He was your mentor too? How lucky were you and how lucky were all of us to serve alongside him and to learn from and work with him. But first, I just want to make a note that Delegate Sickles started off his comments today about his own retirement from this chamber, speaking about others and lifting up the work and the successes of his longtime colleagues and I think

that's all we need to know about his generous spirit and his quick wit.
